title: Where are you from?
goal: Say where you're from, where you live, what you do, and which languages you speak — and meet the basic pattern of Dutch verbs.
bekal: answer *waar kom je vandaan?* and *waar woon je?*
say your job without an article — *ik ben student*, not *een student*
say which languages you speak and how well

dialogs.title: Dialogue — In de pauze
dialogs.intro: A break in class. Sanne comes over with two cups of coffee.

lines.speaker: Budi:

lines.literal: I come out-of Indonesia, out-of Bandung.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.id: And where do you live now?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ik woon in Utrecht, bij mijn tante.
lines.id: I live in Utrecht, at my aunt's.
lines.literal: I live in Utrecht, by my aunt.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Wat doe je hier? Werk je of studeer je?
lines.id: What are you doing here? Do you work or study?

lines.text: Ik studeer. Ik ben student aan de universiteit.
lines.id: I study. I'm a student at the university.

notes: **Waar kom je vandaan?** — note how *vandaan* gets thrown to the end of the sentence. Dutch has many verbs that split up like this (covered fully in Unit 9); for now, learn the question as a whole.
**Ik kom uit Indonesië.** For countries Dutch uses *uit* (out of), not *van*. For cities too: *ik kom uit Bandung*.
**Ik woon in Utrecht** — *wonen* means to live/reside, while *leven* means to be alive. Don't mix them up: *ik leef in Utrecht* sounds as if you're surviving there.
**Ik ben student** — no *een*! This is one of the neatest differences from English (*I am a student*). The article comes back as soon as there is an adjective: *ik ben een goede student*.

**Nee hoor** is the Dutch way to brush off a compliment kindly. The *hoor* at the end of a sentence can't really be translated; it softens the tone, a bit like "really" or "you know": *Dat is goed hoor!*
**Ik spreek een beetje** — *een beetje* (a bit) is a lifesaver in your first months, usually in full as *ik spreek een beetje Nederlands*.

**Ik spreek er maar twee** — *er* here stands for "of them". *Er* is one of the most typically Dutch words and one of the hardest to translate; you will meet it again and again. For now, just recognize its shape.
**Maar** has two meanings: "but" and — as here — "only". Its position decides: at the start of a clause it means "but", in the middle it means "only".

grammars.title: Present-tense verbs: the basic pattern
body: The dictionary form of a Dutch verb ends in **-en**: *wonen*, *werken*, *spreken*. Drop the *-en* and you have the **stem** (the *ik* form): *woon*, *werk*, *spreek*. All that's left is adding *-t* or *-en*.
after: Just three rows. Compare French or Spanish with six different forms — here you really only decide one thing: *-t* or no *-t*. It's English "he works" with a *t* instead of an *s*.

⚠️ One exception you'll meet constantly: when *jij/je* comes **after** the verb (in questions or inverted sentences), that *-t* **disappears**: *je woont* → *woon je?*, *je werkt* → *werk je?* This only applies to *jij/je*, not to *u*: *woont u?*
A stem never ends in a double consonant or in *v/z*: *wonen → woon* (not *won*), *leven → leef*, *reizen → reis*. The reason is spelling, not grammar: the vowel has to stay long.

grammars.title: Countries, nationalities, languages
body: Dutch uses one word for the nationality adjective and the language, and writes it with a **capital letter** — just like English.
after: To talk about speaking a language, the language word stands alone with no article: *ik spreek Nederlands*, *hij leert Engels*.

⚠️ *Holland* is really the name of just two provinces (Noord- and Zuid-Holland). The country is called **Nederland**. The Dutch use both, but outside Holland some people object — and since 2020 the government officially uses only *Nederland*. Also note: *Dutch* in English, but *Duits* in Dutch means **German**!

blocks.text: Many Dutch job words look familiar to English speakers: *student*, *dokter*, *kok* (cook), *chauffeur*. Others are false friends: *winkel* is a **shop** (a *winkelier* runs one), and *kantoor* is an office. If a word looks familiar, it's often a cousin of the English one — but check before you trust it.

blocks.title: Three opening questions you must be able to answer
items: *Wat doe je?* — What do you do? Answer: *Ik ben leraar* / *Ik studeer*.
*Waar werk je?* — Where do you work? Answer: *Ik werk bij Philips* (use **bij** for a company, **in** for a place).
*Wat studeer je?* — What do you study? Answer: *Ik studeer economie / geneeskunde / informatica*.
⚠️ *Wat ben je?* is not the usual job question; it sounds like asking what kind of creature you are.

head: Nederlands
English
rows: Ik versta het wel, maar ik spreek het niet.
I understand it, but I can't speak it.
Could you speak more slowly, please?
Hoe zeg je … in het Nederlands?
How do you say … in Dutch?

blocks.text: *In het Nederlands* — note the *het*: a language name takes an article when it comes after a preposition. *Ik lees het boek in het Engels*.

Here's practical advice you won't find in any grammar book: nearly every Dutch person speaks excellent English, and they will **switch immediately** the moment they hear the slightest hesitation in your sentence. As a native English speaker you'll get this even more. It isn't an insult; it's a habit of being helpful. The rescue line: *Mag ik Nederlands oefenen met u?* — "may I practice my Dutch with you?" Almost nobody says no.
